<reason>Side B (PRO) won a genuinely competitive debate. Side A built a coherent CON case around a purpose-clause argument: since egg donation prevents the disease just as fully, the marginal public pound buys only genetic relatedness plus reversion risk. But B neutralized the categorical premise behind that case with the IVF-with-PGD precedent — public systems already fund precisely the combination of genetic relatedness plus disease prevention, so "public health never buys lineage" fails. A's counter that PGD is "rationed hardest" as a fertility service actually conceded the goal is legitimately funded, and B cleanly turned it: rationing answers how to fund MRT, not whether. B also survived A's sharpest pressure: asked to name a disease outcome MRT delivers that donation does not, B honestly conceded the outcome is the same and reframed around who gets it, anchored in accepted practice. A's homoplasmic-cohort point (the very families needing MRT face the worst reversion risk) was met with a concrete staged-governance threshold and the unanswered natural-conception counterfactual — a small tracked risk versus near-certain untracked transmission. A's best late line, "becomes, not yet is," kept the trial-versus-treatment clash alive, but B's staged funded program with registries plausibly satisfies the motion as written. Execution costs were roughly symmetrical (both had clipped turns). B's rebuttal progression and comparative weighing were marginally stronger, making the debate easier to decide in PRO's favor.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Turn 7 / B4.1: responding to A's trap question ("name one disease outcome MRT delivers that donation doesn't"), B conceded "the disease outcome is the same — the question is who gets it," then anchored MRT in the existing, publicly funded IVF-with-PGD precedent, dissolving A's vaccination-versus-fertility dichotomy and converting A's own concession structure into PRO's decisive comparator.</best_rebuttal>
